source_text: Καὶ γὰρ μυῖαι ἐμπεσοῦσαι μύρῳ, καὶ ἐναποπνιγεῖσαι, ἀσχήμονα τοῦ ἡδέος ἐκείνου χρίσματος, τήν τε ὄψιν, καὶ τὴν χρίσιν ἐργάζονται· σοφίας δὲ καὶ ἀφροσύνης οὐδὲν ἐν ταὐτῷ μεμνῆσθαι προσῆκον. Ὁ μέν γε σοφὸς ἑαυτὸν ἐπὶ δεξιὰ τῶν πραγμάτων ὁδηγεῖ· ἄφρων δὲ εἰς ἀριστερὰ ἀπονένευκεν, οὐδ᾽ ἔστιν ὅτε καλῶν ὁδηγῷ πραγμάτων ἀφροσύνῃ χρήσεται. Μάταια δὲ αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰ ἐνθυμήματα, ἀφροσύνης ἀναπεπλησμένα. Εἰ δὲ καὶ πνεῦμά σοί ποτε, ὦ φίλος, πολέμιον προσπέσοι, ἔνστηθι ἐῤῥωμένως, γινώσκων ὡς καὶ πολλῶν ἁμαρτημάτων πλῆθος Θεὸς ἱλάσασθαι δύναται. Τυράννου δὲ ἔργα ταῦτα, καὶ πατρὸς πάσης πονηρίας· τὸν μὲν ἄφρονα εἰς ὕψος αἴρεσθαι, τὸν πλούσιον δὲ φρονήσει ταπεινοῦσθαι· καὶ δούλους μὲν ἁμαρτιῶν ἐπὶ ἵππον φερομένους, ἄνδρας δὲ ἱεροὺς βαδίζοντας ἀτίμως ὁρᾶσθαι, τῶν πονηρῶν γαυρουμένων.
thought_title: Wisdom and folly; the world turned upside down
orientation: Wisdom and folly cannot be named together, and the father of wickedness raises fools and brings the prudent low.
pass_a_gloss: For flies having fallen into ointment and having been choked/drowned in it, work unseemly both the appearance and the anointing/use of that sweet unguent; but it is fitting that wisdom and folly in no way be mentioned in the same place. The wise man guides himself to the right of affairs; the fool has inclined away to the left, and there is not ever a time when he will use folly as a guide of good affairs. Vain also are his thoughts, filled up with folly. And if a hostile spirit ever falls upon you, O friend, stand against/firm strongly, knowing that God is able to propitiate/pardon even a multitude of many sins. These are works of a tyrant and of the father of all wickedness: the fool to be raised to height, the rich in prudence to be humbled; and slaves of sins borne on a horse, but holy men walking dishonorably to be seen, the wicked exulting.

pass_b_english: For flies that fall into ointment and drown in it make both the look and the use of that sweet anointing unsightly (Ecclesiastes 10:1); but it is not fitting to make any mention of wisdom and folly in the same breath. The wise man guides himself to the right in his affairs, but the fool has turned aside to the left (Ecclesiastes 10:2), and there is never a time when he will use folly as a guide to good things. Even his thoughts are empty, filled with folly (Ecclesiastes 10:3).

If ever a hostile spirit should fall upon you, my friend, stand firm against it with strength, knowing that God is able to pardon even a great multitude of sins (Ecclesiastes 10:4). These are the works of a tyrant and of the father of all wickedness: that the fool is raised on high and the man rich in prudence is brought low (Ecclesiastes 10:5–6); that slaves of sins are seen riding on horseback, while holy men go on foot in dishonor, as the wicked exult (Ecclesiastes 10:7).
notes: Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes 10:1-7. Reads ἐν ταὐτῷ (crasis of τῷ αὐτῷ) as corrected in the source row; rendered 'in the same breath'. χρίσις taken as the act or use of anointing, beside ὄψις 'look'. ἱλάσασθαι with God as subject rendered 'pardon' (the LXX sense of ἱλάσκομαι toward sins, God showing mercy), not 'atone for'; Ecclesiastes 10:4 has 'yielding pacifies great offences'. 'The father of all wickedness' is lowercased: it names the devil, not God; a possible echo of John 8:44 is left uncited. 'Tyrant' renders τυράννου, Gregory's reading of 'the ruler' in Ecclesiastes 10:5. No Psalm citations. 'He will use folly as a guide to good things' follows the 1622 Latin ('nec vnquam ad res praeclaras duce stultitia vtetur'); 'the man rich in prudence' likewise ('prudentiae ... opibus affluentem').
